The above data is a realtime representation of the moon's current status. The data is used as an algorithm to render a custom gradient. 

The gradient's hue follows the phase of the moon: cool blue at new moon, warm gold at full moon. A waxing moon (phase below 0) leans one way and a waning moon (phase above 0) the other. 

Saturation grows with the altitude - 0° means the moon's center is at the horizon, 90° at the zenith (straight over your head). Below the horizon the colors turn darker and more muted. 

Lightness and opacity grow with the illuminated fraction of the moon - 0.0 indicates new moon, 1.0 indicates full moon. 

Without location access the altitude is unknown, so the moon is assumed to be part way up the sky.

To help us improve moonlight, we\'d like to collect anonymous usage data and crash reports. Your location always stays on your device, and no personally identifiable information is collected. You can change this at any time on the about page.

The moon sits in a different part of the sky depending on where you are. moonlight uses your approximate location to work out the moon's position (its azimuth, altitude and distance) from where you stand.

Your location is used only on your device for this calculation. It is never stored or sent anywhere.

Without it, moonlight still shows the moon's phase, but not its position.
moonlight was developed by the artist Jesse Scott and was originally inspired an idea by the artist Kelly Andres.

moonlight is an open source application. \n\nThe code can be found on GitHub and a list of all the libraries used in this project is available below. Special thanks to SunCalc, without which this project would not be possible.
